_comment: Hand-authored layer content merged into layers.json by work/gen_layer_assets.py. Fields: intro (1-sentence, also written to description), about (short explanation for the accordion), links (further reading), period (for static layers, shown instead of From/To), metadata (corrections/overrides).

MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_TrueCol.intro: Natural-color satellite view of Earth as the human eye would see it, with a record back to 2000 — ideal for long-term before/after comparisons.
MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_TrueCol.about: MODIS Corrected Reflectance combines visible bands into a natural-looking image. It is not a science-quality product, but it is designed for visual interpretation and shows smoke, dust and surface features clearly. It is the longest true-color record available in Gibson.

VIIRS_NOAA21_CorrectedReflectance_TrueCo.intro: Today's natural-color view of Earth from the newest VIIRS satellite — the sharpest daily imagery for recent events.
VIIRS_NOAA21_CorrectedReflectance_TrueCo.about: VIIRS Corrected Reflectance from NOAA-21 (JPSS-2), the current-generation polar orbiter. It is higher resolution than MODIS, updated daily, and is the default base layer for recent dates.

IMERG_Precipitation_Rate.intro: Global rainfall estimates from the GPM mission, archived back to 2000 — use it to reconstruct a specific past storm or flood event.
IMERG_Precipitation_Rate.about: IMERG merges microwave and infrared observations from the GPM Core Observatory and partner satellites into a 10 km global rain map every 30 minutes. The archive lets you replay any storm since June 2000.

IMERG_Precipitation_Rate_30min.intro: Near-real-time global rainfall, updated every 30 minutes — the 'is it raining there today' layer.
IMERG_Precipitation_Rate_30min.about: The near-real-time IMERG product covers only the last few days. Use it to track active storms, monsoons and rainfall anomalies as they happen.

MODIS_Terra_L3_NDVI_Monthly.intro: Monthly vegetation greenness index since 2000 — spot crop stress, greening and browning trends season by season.
MODIS_Terra_L3_NDVI_Monthly.about: NDVI measures how much near-infrared light vegetation reflects: healthy plants are bright, stressed or sparse vegetation is dark. The monthly composite removes most cloud noise, making it the best layer for year-to-year comparisons.

VIIRS_NOAA20_NDVI_8Day.intro: Current 8-day vegetation greenness from VIIRS — fresher than the monthly layer for fast-moving stories.
VIIRS_NOAA20_NDVI_8Day.about: The 8-day NDVI composite from NOAA-20 VIIRS updates every 8 days, so it shows vegetation stress sooner than the monthly product.

MODIS_Combined_Value_Added_AOD.intro: Global aerosol (dust, smoke, haze) concentration from MODIS — the layer for Saharan dust and biomass-burning smoke stories.
MODIS_Combined_Value_Added_AOD.about: Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) measures how much sunlight airborne particles block: high values mean dusty or smoky air. MODIS combines Terra and Aqua observations for daily global coverage.

TROPOMI_L2_Nitrogen_Dioxide_Tropospheric.intro: Nitrogen dioxide pollution from traffic, industry and fires, measured daily by the Sentinel-5P satellite.
TROPOMI_L2_Nitrogen_Dioxide_Tropospheric.about: TROPOMI maps the tropospheric NO₂ column at ~7 km resolution. NO₂ is a key marker of combustion — urban pollution, power plants and biomass burning all show up clearly.

TROPOMI_L2_Sulfur_Dioxide_Total_Vertical.intro: Sulfur dioxide from volcanoes and industry, measured daily by Sentinel-5P — watch eruptions and power-plant emissions.
TROPOMI_L2_Sulfur_Dioxide_Total_Vertical.about: TROPOMI measures the total vertical column of SO₂. Large signals come from volcanic eruptions (e.g. Nyiragongo) and from smelters and power plants.

MODIS_Combined_Thermal_Anomalies_All.intro: Active fire detections from MODIS with a record back to 2002 — compare today's fires with previous years.
MODIS_Combined_Thermal_Anomalies_All.about: MODIS detects thermal anomalies (fires) day and night at 1 km resolution. It is the longest fire record in Gibson, ideal for 'is this worse than previous years' stories.

VIIRS_NOAA20_Thermal_Anomalies_375m_All.intro: The flagship active-fire layer — 375 m fire detections from VIIRS, day and night, updated daily.
VIIRS_NOAA20_Thermal_Anomalies_375m_All.about: VIIRS detects fires at 375 m — sharper than MODIS — making it the headline wildfire layer for current events.

VIIRS_NOAA21_Thermal_Anomalies_375m_All.intro: VIIRS fire detections from NOAA-21, adding an extra daily overpass for more complete coverage.
VIIRS_NOAA21_Thermal_Anomalies_375m_All.about: Same product family as the NOAA-20 fire layer, from the newer NOAA-21 satellite. Together the two satellites catch more fires per day.

VIIRS_SNPP_Thermal_Anomalies_375m_All.intro: VIIRS fire detections from the original Suomi NPP satellite — the longest VIIRS fire record (since 2012).
VIIRS_SNPP_Thermal_Anomalies_375m_All.about: The oldest VIIRS platform, providing the longest VIIRS fire record and maximum daily coverage when combined with the other VIIRS satellites.

VIIRS_NOAA20_CorrectedReflectance_BandsM.intro: False-color imagery that makes burn scars glow orange-red — show cumulative fire damage, not just today's detections.
VIIRS_NOAA20_CorrectedReflectance_BandsM.about: The M11-I2-I1 band combination highlights burned ground. Use it alongside the active-fire points to show the full extent of a fire season.

MODIS_Combined_Flood_1-Day.intro: Daily flood extent from MODIS — the best-resolution flood layer for historical African floods (e.g. 2022 Nigeria).
MODIS_Combined_Flood_1-Day.about: MODIS flood detection maps surface water at 250 m. The 1-day product is the sharpest; use it for historical events like the 2022 Nigeria floods, Lake Chad and the Sudd.

MODIS_Combined_Flood_2-Day.intro: Two-day flood composite from MODIS — balances coverage and cloud reduction for historical flood maps.
MODIS_Combined_Flood_2-Day.about: Combines two days of MODIS flood detections to reduce cloud false-positives while keeping good temporal detail.

MODIS_Combined_Flood_3-Day.intro: Three-day flood composite from MODIS — the cleanest historical flood maps, with fewer cloud gaps.
MODIS_Combined_Flood_3-Day.about: Averages three days of detections to minimise cloud false-positives. Best for clean, presentation-ready historical flood maps.

VIIRS_Combined_Flood_1-Day.intro: Near-real-time flood extent at 375 m from VIIRS — the 'impact' layer for current flooding (data from 2025 onward).
VIIRS_Combined_Flood_1-Day.about: VIIRS flood detection at 375 m, updated daily. Note: this layer only has data from mid-2025 — for older floods use the MODIS flood layers.

VIIRS_Combined_Flood_2-Day.intro: Two-day VIIRS flood composite — near-real-time flood extent with fewer cloud false-positives.
VIIRS_Combined_Flood_2-Day.about: Combines two days of VIIRS flood detections. Data from mid-2025 onward.

VIIRS_Combined_Flood_3-Day.intro: Three-day VIIRS flood composite — the cleanest recent flood maps from the current-generation satellites.
VIIRS_Combined_Flood_3-Day.about: Averages three days of VIIRS detections. Data from mid-2025 onward.

OPERA_L3_Dynamic_Surface_Water_Extent-Se.intro: 30 m flood mapping from radar — sees through clouds, so it works even during active rain and heavy cloud cover.
OPERA_L3_Dynamic_Surface_Water_Extent-Se.about: OPERA's Dynamic Surface Water Extent from Sentinel-1 SAR penetrates clouds and works day and night. It is the only near-real-time flood layer that works during active storms. Zoom to level 10+ for full detail.

OPERA_L3_Dynamic_Surface_Water_Extent-HL.intro: 30 m water mapping from Landsat and Sentinel-2 — the sharpest optical flood layer, updated near-daily.
OPERA_L3_Dynamic_Surface_Water_Extent-HL.about: OPERA's Dynamic Surface Water Extent from Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) detects rivers, lakes, reservoirs and floodplains at 30 m. Zoom to level 10+ for full detail.

NDH_Flood_Hazard_Frequency_Distribution_.intro: Historical flood hazard map (1985–2003) — see where floods have repeatedly occurred, as context for recent events.
NDH_Flood_Hazard_Frequency_Distribution_.about: A static risk layer from the Natural Disaster Hotspots project showing how often floods struck each area over 1985–2003. Compare recent floods against this historical baseline.

MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_Bands72.intro: False-color imagery where water appears dark and vegetation bright — a classic way to map flood extent.
MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_Bands72.about: Water absorbs near- and shortwave-infrared, so open water and flooded ground appear very dark in this 7-2-1 composite while vegetation stays bright green. Daily since 2000.

VIIRS_SNPP_CorrectedReflectance_BandsM11.intro: Sharper 375 m false-color imagery for flood mapping — water is dark, vegetation is bright.
VIIRS_SNPP_CorrectedReflectance_BandsM11.about: The M11-I2-I1 band combination from VIIRS at 375 m. Water and flooded ground appear dark while vegetation is bright — useful for delineating flood extent and vegetation stress. Daily since 2015.

GRACE_Tellus_Liquid_Water_Equivalent_Thi.intro: Monthly changes in total water storage (including deep groundwater) from the GRACE satellites — the only way to see aquifers from space.
GRACE_Tellus_Liquid_Water_Equivalent_Thi.about: GRACE measures shifts in Earth's gravity caused by moving water. The ~300 km resolution is coarse, but it is the only satellite product that sees deep aquifer depletion — ideal for basin-scale stories like Lake Chad or the Nile.

MODIS_Terra_L3_Land_Surface_Temp_Daily_D.intro: Daily daytime land-surface temperature from MODIS — the heat-stress companion to soil moisture.
MODIS_Terra_L3_Land_Surface_Temp_Daily_D.about: Land surface temperature (LST) shows how hot the ground actually is. Anomalously high temperatures accompany drought and heat stress on vegetation.

SMAP_L3_Passive_Day_Soil_Moisture.intro: Daily surface soil moisture (0–5 cm) from SMAP — responds fast to rainfall deficits, ideal for single-season drought stories.
SMAP_L3_Passive_Day_Soil_Moisture.about: SMAP measures the microwave signal of water in the top 5 cm of soil at ~36 km resolution. It reacts quickly to dry spells, making it the go-to layer for tracking a drought as it develops.

BlueMarble_NextGeneration.intro: A static, cloud-free view of Earth — a clean fallback base when daily imagery is patchy.
BlueMarble_NextGeneration.about: NASA's Blue Marble Next Generation composite of MODIS imagery, showing the planet without clouds. Loads at a fixed resolution.

OpenStreetMap.intro: Familiar street-map tiles for context when satellite imagery isn't needed.

Coastlines.intro: Global coastline outlines — a simple reference overlay for orientation.
Coastlines.about: Coastlines from OpenStreetMap and the SCAR Antarctic Digital Database. Date-independent, always available.

Reference_Labels.intro: City and country names on the map.
Reference_Labels.about: GIBS reference labels for places and countries. Date-independent.

Reference_Features.intro: Political borders and major feature lines.

OSM_Land_Mask.intro: Darkens the oceans to make land stand out.
OSM_Land_Mask.about: An OpenStreetMap-derived land/ocean mask used as an underlay. Date-independent.

GOES-East_ABI_GeoColor.intro: Natural-colour view of the Americas and Atlantic, a new frame every 10 minutes. The layer for tracking hurricanes and storms as they happen — a night-time component keeps them visible after dark.
GOES-East_ABI_GeoColor.about: GOES-East sits over the equator at 75°W watching one hemisphere continuously, so unlike the polar-orbiting daily layers it can show a storm growing hour by hour. GeoColor is a natural-colour composite with a night-time component (city lights, fires and low cloud), which means a hurricane or a dust plume stays visible overnight. Outside the satellite's disk there is no data — that part of the map shows the base layer only.

GOES-West_ABI_GeoColor.intro: Natural-colour view of the eastern Pacific and western Americas, refreshed every 10 minutes — Pacific storm systems and hurricanes closing on Mexico or the US.
GOES-West_ABI_GeoColor.about: GOES-West watches the eastern Pacific from 137°W. Same 10-minute GeoColor product as its eastern twin, pointed at the other half of the Americas' weather.

Himawari_AHI_Band3_Red_Visible_1km.intro: Daylight natural-colour view of Asia and the western Pacific, a new frame every 10 minutes — typhoon and monsoon tracking at 1 km.
Himawari_AHI_Band3_Red_Visible_1km.about: Himawari-9 (Japan Meteorological Agency) watches Asia and the western Pacific from 140.7°E. This is its red visible band: sharp 1 km daylight imagery, but unlike GeoColor it shows nothing at night.

GOES-East_ABI_Band13_Clean_Infrared.intro: Cloud-top temperatures over the Americas and Atlantic every 10 minutes. The coldest tops are the tallest, most intense storms — and it works day and night.
GOES-East_ABI_Band13_Clean_Infrared.about: Clean Infrared (band 13, 10.3 µm) measures the temperature of whatever the satellite sees: the colder the top, the higher and more violent the cloud. That makes it the standard way to judge storm intensity — and unlike visible imagery it keeps working after sunset, when many storms peak.

GOES-West_ABI_Band13_Clean_Infrared.intro: Cloud-top temperatures over the eastern Pacific every 10 minutes — storm intensity day and night for Pacific systems.
GOES-West_ABI_Band13_Clean_Infrared.about: The infrared twin of the GOES-East cloud-top layer, watching the eastern Pacific. Cold, high cloud tops show where a system is deepening; the imagery is unaffected by the day/night line.

Himawari_AHI_Band13_Clean_Infrared.intro: Cloud-top temperatures over Asia and the western Pacific every 10 minutes — typhoon intensity, day or night.
Himawari_AHI_Band13_Clean_Infrared.about: Himawari's infrared band, refreshed every 10 minutes. Where the visible band goes dark, this one keeps showing the structure of a typhoon or a monsoon surge.
